How is a Trump Account taxed when you withdraw money?

The seed deposit and contribution caps are the easy part. The part that catches people off guard is what happens on the way out -- the account is taxed like a traditional IRA, not like the 529 plan most savers are picturing. Three worked examples below, all pinned to this calculator's own arithmetic.

Worked example 1: withdrawing at 18, for a use that isn't on the recognized list

A US citizen born 2026 (seed-eligible), family contributes $5,000/year for 18 years, 6% annual return, 12% marginal tax rate, withdrawn at 18 for something other than education, a first home, disability, or similar.

LineAmount
Balance at withdrawal$166,654.30
Basis (family contributions only)$90,000.00
Tax-free share of the balance54.0%
Tax-free amount$90,000.00
Taxable amount (seed + growth)$76,654.30
Income tax on the taxable amount (12%)$9,198.52
10% early-withdrawal penalty$7,665.43
Net after tax and penalty$149,790.35

Turning 18 unlocks the ability to withdraw at all -- it does not by itself avoid the 10% penalty. That still applies to the taxable portion of any withdrawal before age 59 1/2, unless the withdrawal is for a recognized use.

Worked example 2: the same withdrawal, for a recognized use

Identical numbers to example 1 -- same balance, same basis, same 54.0% tax-free split -- except this withdrawal is for a use the traditional-IRA penalty exceptions already recognize (qualified higher education, a first home purchase, certain disability, and similar).

LineAmount
Tax-free amount$90,000.00
Taxable amount$76,654.30
Income tax on the taxable amount (12%)$9,198.52
10% early-withdrawal penalty$0.00 (waived)
Net after tax and penalty$157,455.78

A recognized use waives the $7,665.43 penalty -- $7,665.43 more than example 1 -- but does not waive the $9,198.52 income tax on the taxable portion. Only a 529 plan waives tax on withdrawal for a qualified use; a Trump Account never does.

Worked example 3: the same balance, but with employer money instead of family money

Same total contribution room used, same 18 years, same 6% return, same $166,654.30 balance -- but $2,500/year of the $5,000/year comes from an employer (under the shared cap) instead of all $5,000/year coming from the family.

LineAll-familyHalf-employer
Balance$166,654.30$166,654.30
Basis (family only)$90,000.00$45,000.00
Non-basis (seed + employer)$1,000.00$46,000.00
Tax-free share of every withdrawal54.0%27.0%

Same balance, same total dollars contributed -- but the tax-free fraction is cut in half, because an employer's contribution creates no basis at all. It is taxed exactly like the seed deposit and the investment growth: fully taxable on withdrawal, unlike the identical dollar amount coming from a family member.

Run this with your own numbers

The Trump Account calculator applies this same pro-rata arithmetic to any current age, contribution mix, return rate, tax rate, and withdrawal age you enter, and shows the tax-free/taxable split, the penalty, and the net after-tax amount. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Common questions

On an $166,654 balance with $90,000 of family contributions, how much comes out tax-free?

54.0% of ANY withdrawal -- $90,000 is basis (the family's own contributions) out of a $166,654 total balance, and the IRA pro-rata rule applies that same 54.0%/45.0% split to every dollar withdrawn, not just the first dollars out.

Does withdrawing at 18 avoid the 10% early-withdrawal penalty?

No -- turning 18 only unlocks the ability to withdraw at all. The 10% penalty still applies to the taxable portion of a withdrawal before age 59 1/2 unless the withdrawal is for a recognized use (qualified education, a first home, certain disability, and similar). On the $166,654 example, withdrawing at 18 for an unrecognized use costs $9,198.52 in income tax plus a $7,665.43 penalty -- withdrawing the same balance for a recognized use waives the $7,665.43 penalty and leaves the $9,198.52 income tax due either way.

Does it matter whether the same dollars come from a family member or an employer?

Yes, a lot. Swap $2,500/year of a $5,000/year family contribution for a $2,500/year employer contribution instead -- same total money in, same $166,654 balance -- and the tax-free fraction falls from 54.0% to 27.0%, because employer contributions create no basis at all. Every dollar an employer puts in is treated like investment growth: fully taxable on withdrawal, unlike the identical dollar amount coming from a family member.

TRUMP ACCOUNT CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What will a Trump Account be worth, and how much of it is actually yours?

A Trump Account is the new federal child savings account created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act: a one-time $1,000 seed deposit for a US citizen born 2025-2028, plus up to $5,000/year in combined family and employer money. This projects the balance to age 18 or later, and shows the withdrawal split almost every 529-plan comparison gets wrong: only your own contributions come out tax-free — the seed money, employer contributions, and every dollar of growth do not.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. The child's account

2. Annual contributions

Family and employer money together cannot exceed $5,000/year (the 2026-2027 figure), and the employer portion alone cannot exceed $2,500/year — this projection applies both caps and this same dollar amount every year until the withdrawal age above.

3. Withdrawal

Fill in the account and contribution details, then click Calculate.

Projection

What this does not cover

  • Not a full tax return. This estimates one account's federal tax treatment only — not your total tax liability, other deductions or credits, or state tax (most states have not yet ruled on their own treatment of a Trump Account).
  • Citizenship and birth year are self-reported — confirmed by you, not verified here.
  • The $5,000 annual cap is applied flat to every projected year. By statute it is indexed upward in $100 increments starting 2028, so this understates the room available in later years — never overstates it.
  • Assumes a single, full withdrawal at the chosen age. A series of partial withdrawals uses the same pro-rata percentage on each one, applied to a shrinking balance.

Common questions

What is a Trump Account?

A federal, tax-advantaged savings account for a US citizen under 18, created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (26 U.S.C. 530A). A US citizen born 2025-2028 gets a one-time $1,000 federal pilot deposit; anyone can then contribute up to $5,000/year combined (2026-2027, indexed from 2028), invested in a fund tracking a broad US-company index. No distributions of any kind are allowed before the account owner turns 18.

Is the $1,000 seed deposit taxed the same as money I contribute myself?

No -- and this is the detail a 529-plan comparison gets backwards. Money YOU (or another individual) contribute is basis and comes out tax-free. The $1,000 federal seed deposit and any employer contribution create NO basis: every dollar of those, plus ALL investment growth on the whole account, is taxed as ordinary income when withdrawn.

Can I withdraw just my own contributions tax-free and leave the taxable part in the account?

No. Withdrawals follow the IRA pro-rata rule: every withdrawal is part tax-free and part taxable, in the same ratio as your basis is to the total account value. You cannot choose to take out your own contributions first.

How much can an employer contribute, and does it count against the $5,000 limit?

An employer can exclude up to $2,500/year per employee from that employee's federal taxable income (still generally subject to payroll tax), and that $2,500 counts INSIDE the shared $5,000 annual cap, not on top of it -- so a $2,500 employer contribution leaves only $2,500 of room for everyone else that year.

What happens if I withdraw before age 18, or before 59.5?

No distribution of any kind is permitted before the account owner turns 18. From 18 on, the account is taxed like a traditional IRA: a 10% penalty applies to the taxable portion of any withdrawal before age 59.5, unless the withdrawal is for a use the traditional-IRA penalty exceptions already recognize -- qualified higher education expenses, a first home purchase, certain disability, and similar.

Is this tax advice?

No. This calculator applies the published federal contribution caps, seed-deposit rule, and pro-rata withdrawal formula to the numbers you enter. It is not a full tax return, it does not verify your child's citizenship or birth year, and it is not a substitute for reviewing the IRS's own guidance or consulting a qualified tax professional.

This calculator vs. working out a Trump Account by hand

A Trump Account looks like simple arithmetic — a seed deposit, a contribution cap, a growth rate. The problem is that its withdrawal treatment does not resemble the other child-savings vehicle most people already know, a 529 plan, and a quick by-hand estimate tends to borrow that plan's rules by habit.

Where a hand estimate usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Withdrawal taxationAssumes the whole balance is tax-free for a qualified use, generalizing from a 529 plan.Applies the IRA-style pro-rata rule: only individual contributions are basis and come out tax-free; the seed, employer money, and all growth are taxed as ordinary income.
Which dollars come out firstAssumes you can withdraw your own tax-free contributions first, leaving taxable money in the account.Applies the same tax-free/taxable ratio to every withdrawal, exactly as the pro-rata rule requires.
The $2,500 employer sub-capTreats it as $2,500 of room on top of the $5,000 total, for $7,500 combined.Applies the employer's $2,500 sub-cap INSIDE the shared $5,000 annual limit, and shows the room left for everyone else.
Early accessAssumes at least the family's own contributions can be withdrawn before 18 if needed.Applies the statutory rule directly: no distribution of any kind before age 18, regardless of who contributed it.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the single most common mistake working this out by hand?

Assuming a Trump Account works like a 529 plan, where the whole balance comes out tax-free for a qualified use. It does not -- only money an individual contributed is basis and comes out tax-free; the $1,000 seed deposit, any employer contribution, and every dollar of investment growth are taxed as ordinary income on withdrawal, no matter what the money is used for.

What's the second most common mistake?

Assuming you can choose to withdraw your own tax-free contributions first and leave the taxable money sitting in the account. The IRA pro-rata rule does not allow that -- every withdrawal is part tax-free and part taxable, in the same ratio as your basis is to the total account value, every time, until the account is empty.

What contribution-cap mistake gets made most often?

Treating the $2,500 employer contribution limit as separate from the $5,000 total. It is not additional room -- an employer's $2,500 counts INSIDE the shared $5,000 annual cap, so it leaves only $2,500 for everyone else that year, not $5,000.

What withdrawal-timing mistake gets made most often?

Assuming the account works like a custodial brokerage account that a parent can tap early if needed. No distribution of any kind -- not even of money the family contributed -- is permitted before the account owner turns 18, and a hand estimate often assumes at least the family's own contributions could be pulled out sooner.

Does this calculator know my complete tax situation?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page knows your full return -- other deductions, credits, or state tax treatment, which most states have not yet ruled on for a Trump Account. Both apply the same published federal seed-deposit rule, contribution caps, and pro-rata withdrawal formula to the numbers you enter; verify against the IRS's own guidance or a qualified tax professional before relying on either.
